title: Rapid Frontline Operator Cookbook and Incident Play Cards
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Summary:
This compact cookbook is a frontline operator reference for the first 30 minutes of an incident. It is intentionally concise: a set of distilled play cards, triage checklists, escalation timeboxes, and customer/status messaging templates designed for rapid execution during high-pressure incidents affecting LLM inference (latency, errors, quality regressions, capacity blips). Use this as a pocket guide during the bridge and as the canonical short-form source for responder quick training.

Scope and intent:
- Scope: incidents impacting Redwood-hosted inference or Dedicated pools where operator actions can materially reduce customer impact within the first 30 minutes.
- Intent: reduce cognitive load for first responders; provide deterministic next steps and safe fallbacks; accelerate evidence collection for postmortem.

How to use this document:
1) Identify the play card that best matches the observed symptoms.
2) Run the triage check list for that card in parallel with status updates.
3) Escalate according to the ladder if thresholds/timeboxes are met.
4) After stabilization, attach logs and timeline to the incident channel and trigger postmortem template.

Operational primitives (commands and links):
- Bridge creation (Slack): /incident start --service=redwood-inference --severity=sev2 --lead=@oncall
- Pager to bridge quick link: https://redwood.ops/bridges/new?service=inference
- SLO dashboard: https://console.redwood/slo/inference
- Common CLI checks (run from ops-jump host):
  - Check fleet health: redwoodctl fleet status --service inference --region us-west-2
  - Check queue/backpressure: redwoodctl metrics query "requests.backlog{service=inference}" --last 15m
  - Inspect model-serving pods: kubectl get pods -n inference -l workload=model-serving -o wide
  - Tail model server logs: kubectl logs -f <pod> -n inference --container model-runtime | grep -E "ERROR|WARN|evict|throttle"
  - Restart transient worker: kubectl rollout restart deployment/model-runtime -n inference --to-revision=<rev>

Roles and responsibilities (quick):
- Bridge owner: coordinates comms, assigns roles, updates status page.
- Primary responder: executes triage and mitigation play card.
- Escalation engineer: implements hotfixes (config change, model switch, restart).
- Customer comms lead: drafts and posts status updates and customer-facing messages.
- Evidence scribe: collects timeline, logs, traces for postmortem.

Escalation ladder (timeboxed):
- 0-5m: Acknowledge pager, confirm symptoms, create bridge. Primary responder runs Play Card A (basic triage).
- 5-15m: If no stabilizing action, escalate to escalation engineer; prepare customer status draft.
- 15-30m: If impact persists or SLO > 5% breached for > 15m, escalate to on-call SRE lead and Product on-call for comms; consider partial mitigation (model fallback, capacity fallback).
- >30m: If unresolved, declare Sev1 and involve Exec on-call and Incident Commander.

Play cards (choose one, follow steps in order). Each card has: trigger, quick checks (evidence), mitigation steps, rollback, follow-up evidence to collect.

Play Card A: Latency spike (sustained P99 > 2x baseline)
- Trigger: Alert from SLO engine or customer complaint; P99 latency doubled for last 5m.
- Quick checks (0-5m):
  1. Confirm region/cluster: SLO dashboard -> region.
  2. Check pod health & OOMs: kubectl get pods -n inference -o wide; kubectl describe pod <pod> if restarts>0.
  3. Check GPU saturation: redwoodctl gpu metrics --cluster <cluster> --last 10m.
- Immediate mitigations (5-15m):
  1. Enable autoscale burst if available: redwoodctl capacity burst --pool inference-primary --scale-to 20
  2. If autoscale unavailable, switch traffic to a lower-latency model variant: console -> routes -> create temporary route "fallback-low-latency" -> point 20% traffic.
  3. Throttle large requests by rate-limit policy: rctl apply --policy=thin-request-throttle
- Rollback steps:
  - If latency normalizes, revert temporary route and remove burst within 10m. Monitor for oscillations.
- Evidence to collect:
  - pod logs, gpu metrics, request traces for noisy clients, route change record.

Play Card B: KV cache eviction / prefix-cache miss storm
- Trigger: Sudden spike in request latency for short prompts; cache hit ratio drops 30% -> 5%
- Quick checks:
  1. Check cache service metrics: redis-hitrate: redwoodctl metrics query "kv.cache.hitrate" --last 15m
  2. Check eviction logs: kubectl logs cache-0 -n inference | tail 200
- Immediate mitigations:
  1. Increase cache TTL from 60s -> 300s for affected model: etcdctl put /configs/kv/ttl 300 --prefix=production
  2. Enable best-effort prefix caching on serving nodes: redwoodctl feature enable prefix-caching --scope=inference --duration=30m
  3. Temporarily divert heavy clients to a cold-path with lower QPS: route-based holdback.
- Rollback: revert TTL to previous value after 1 hour and observe hitrate returning.
- Evidence: cache metrics, eviction counters, request client IDs.

Play Card C: Model quality regression (sudden increase in hallucinations/incorrect outputs)
- Trigger: Customer report + monitoring evals showing >10% drop against golden prompt set in last deployment.
- Quick checks:
  1. Confirm model version: console -> deployments -> model-serving -> current-version
  2. Run golden prompt nanobench: curl -X POST https://local-eval/redwood -d '{"prompts": [..]}'
  3. Check rollout percentage: console -> rollouts
- Immediate mitigations:
  1. Rollback to previous model version: console -> rollback -> confirm.
  2. If rollback unavailable, enable deterministic decoding settings (temperature->0.2) at route level.
  3. Put an alerts-only fence: route -> require review for generations > 2048 tokens.
- Rollback: If decoding change causes regressions, revert to prior decode settings and initiate hotfix plan.
- Evidence: evaluation run, model artifacts, commit hashes, rollout logs.

Play Card D: Capacity exhaustion / noisy neighbor on Dedicated pool
- Trigger: spike in queue depth, request timeouts, high GPU utilization in a Dedicated pool.
- Quick checks:
  1. View pool utilization: redwoodctl pool usage --pool dedicated-eu-1 --last 10m
  2. Identify recent tenant changes: audit logs -> who triggered heavy jobs in last 30m.
- Immediate mitigations:
  1. Activate tenant throttling: redwoodctl tenant throttle --tenant <id> --qps 10
  2. Evacuate low-priority workloads: move batch jobs to fallback queue.
  3. Enable capacity overflow routing to hosted: route policy -> overflow->hosted-region-us-east.
- Follow-up: open a billing/usage review with customer-success if tenant was misconfigured.

Customer and status page messaging templates (short-form). Use these verbatim for the first 3 updates. Customize bracketed fields.
- Initial acknowledgement (within 10m):
  "We are investigating reports of elevated latency impacting Redwood Inference in [region]. Our engineers have created an incident bridge and are actively triaging. We will post an update within 15 minutes. Affected customers may see increased generation latency or timeouts. — Redwood Ops"
- Status update (15m):
  "Update: We identified increased GPU saturation in [cluster]. We have applied a traffic diversion to a fallback pool and are monitoring for stabilization. Some requests may still see higher latency. Next update in 30 minutes or earlier if conditions change."
- Customer-facing resolution (post-stable):
  "Resolved: The immediate issue affecting inference latency in [region] has been mitigated by traffic diversion and autoscale adjustments. We are now rolling back temporary configurations and will monitor for recurrence. We will publish a post-incident summary within 72 hours. For customers who experienced extended impact, our support team will reach out with account-specific details."

Post-incident: immediate actions (first 24 hours)
1. Convert bridge notes to an incident ticket in our tracker: /incident export --bridge <id> --to=JIRA-INF-<num>
2. Evidence package: attach logs (pod, gpu, cache), traces, SLO graphs, route changes.
3. Assign postmortem owner (should not be bridge owner unless otherwise agreed).
4. Draft timeline with minute-level granularity for first 30 minutes.
5. Publish a short customer-facing incident note within 72 hours.

Postmortem template (short):
- Title: [Service] Incident YYYY-MM-DD – short cause summary
- Incident lead: <name>
- Severity: Sev1/2/3
- Summary (1–3 sentences):
- Impact: affected regions/customers/SLO impact numbers
- Root cause: one-paragraph technical cause
- Contributing factors: list
- Corrective actions (owner + due date): bullet list
- Preventative actions (owner + due date): bullet list
- Evidence: links to logs/traces/dashboards
- Follow-up review date: YYYY-MM-DD

Game day quick plan (2-hour lab):
- Objective: practice the decisions in this cookbook for two incident types: (1) latency spike and (2) model-regression.
- Participants: 1 bridge conductor, 2 primary responders, 1 comms lead, 1 observer (evidence scribe).
- Timeline:
  - 0–5m: Trigger and bridge creation.
  - 5–20m: Execute play card, collect evidence.
  - 20–40m: Escalation scenario where mitigation fails; practice traffic fallback.
  - 40–60m: Stabilization and rollback.
  - 60–120m: Postmortem write-up and 15-minute retro.
- Scoring (pass/fail quick):
  - Bridge created <5m (pass), customer message posted <15m (pass), rollback completed <30m if required (pass).

Shift handover ritual (2-minute checklist for outgoing oncall):
- Current active incidents and bridge links.
- SLOs near threshold (list).
- Any in-flight rollouts or config changes (link + expected completion).
- Customers to watch (list).
- Pager silence confirmations and escalation contacts updated.

Runbook ownership and maintenance policy:
- Each play card must have an owning team and an annual review date. Play cards with more than 3 activations in 90 days must be escalated to a reliability initiative.
- How to update: fork the play card page, propose change, add reviewer, and mark status=in_review.

Appendix: quick-reference thresholds table
| Symptom | Alert threshold | Action window | Escalate if not resolved |
| Latency P99 > baseline *2 | 5m sustained | 15m | 30m -> Sev1 if >5% SLO loss |
| Cache hitrate drop >30% | 5m | 30m | 60m |
| Model eval drop >10% | 5m | 15m | 30m -> rollback |
| Pool GPU util > 90% and queue>100 | 5m | 10m | 20m -> tenant throttle |

Appendix: useful links and runbooks
- Full runbook library: https://confluence.redwood/inference/runbooks
- Incident evidence standard: https://confluence.redwood/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-evidence-chain-and-forensic-runbook-2025
- Playbook provenance and change log: https://confluence.redwood/oncall-and-incident-response/playbook-provenance

Notes and rationale:
This document is intentionally action-first. Detailed root-cause analysis, long-term remediation plans, and deep forensic procedures live in the runbook library linked above. The goal here is to make front-line operators fast and confident when acting under pressure, while ensuring the incident remains auditable and evidence-rich for later follow-up.
